courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Training: the loss, clone, split, prune and opacity reset
md: Densification is driven by the *positional* gradient, not by the photometric error at a pixel directly. A region can look wrong yet not densify if its Gaussians are not being pushed around, which is one reason poorly observed regions stay blurry.

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: One final score hides where the gain came from
md: An ablation turns one end-to-end number into a per-component account: what each stage adds, on the same queries and labels, under the same settings. Without it, you cannot tell which stage earns its latency.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
md: Outcome grading is not the same as correct behavior. A grader only sees what it checks: tests that cover one interpretation, a database diff, an answer string. Anything outside the check (rudeness, a policy step skipped, an unrelated file deleted) can pass silently.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Keeping the context window under control
md: Compaction is lossy. The Agent SDK docs warn that specific instructions from early in the conversation may not survive a summary. Put durable rules in a file that is re-injected on every request (the SDK uses CLAUDE.md for this), not only in the first user message.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: Evaluating memory and the ways it fails
md: Memory is untrusted input that outlives the session. Record provenance on every write (user said it, a tool returned it, the model inferred it), only promote user-stated facts to instructions-like status, show retrieved memories to the model as quoted data, and give users a way to view and delete what the agent remembers.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Multi-turn rollouts: one sequence, two authors, one loss mask
md: A common bug: tokenizing the final transcript string again for training instead of keeping the exact token ids that were sampled. Re-tokenizing can merge tokens differently at the boundaries between model text and tool text, so the log-probabilities you train on no longer match the ones the policy produced, and the mask can land on the wrong positions.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
md: Materials generators are diffusion models over a mixed object (types, periodic coordinates, lattice). They change where candidates come from; MLIPs and DFT still decide which are stable, and novelty must be checked against experimental databases.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks, limits, and content credentials for images
md: Watermarks are statistical evidence woven into content; content credentials are signed claims attached to a file. Metadata is easy to strip but cryptographically strong; watermarks survive some edits but can be scrubbed, spoofed or never applied. Real deployments combine them.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Isolation Forest: anomalies split off in fewer random cuts
md: Isolation Forest scores a point by how few random axis-parallel cuts it takes to isolate it, normalized by c(n). It is fast (training is O(t psi log psi) and needs no distances), works on a small subsample, and is strongest for global anomalies far from all the data.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: LSNs, pageLSN and the two tables recovery rebuilds
md: Do not mix up pageLSN and recLSN. In the example, P1 was first dirtied at LSN 10 and last changed at 60, so its recLSN is 10 while its pageLSN is 60. recLSN says where redo for the page might need to start; pageLSN says which changes the page already contains.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: A toy run: how the input type flips the top result
md: Simplified: real embeddings are not interpretable feature lists, and the size of the effect varies by model and corpus. The toy shows the direction of the failure, not its typical magnitude. Lesson 5 is about measuring the magnitude on your data.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: One API in front of many models: the Converse call
md: `inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Training from scratch: latent weights and the STE
md: Training a BitNet is not cheaper than training an FP16 model with today's code. Latent weights, gradients and optimizer states are high precision, and the FAQ notes their training ran in FP16/BF16 with no speedup. The savings are at inference.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Branchless code: cmov, masks and lookup tables
md: `cmov` with a memory operand always reads memory, even when the condition is false (the Intel pseudocode does `temp := SRC` first and lists page faults as possible). So a compiler cannot turn `p ? *p : 0` into a cmov from `*p`: it would fault on a null pointer. C's `?:` only evaluates the chosen side; branchless code evaluates both.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Leveled vs tiered compaction: counting write, read and space cost
md: Leveled: low space and read amplification, high write amplification. Tiered: low write amplification, more runs to read and up to about 2x temporary space during a full merge. The size ratio T slides each policy along its curve.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive
md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: Tools such as AddressSanitizer and fuzzing find many of these bugs, but only on inputs that actually run. The Android team describes them as treating symptoms rather than the root cause, and notes that coverage stays low without constant pressure on teams to fuzz and triage.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Why one load can cost 3 cycles or 240
md: Latency numbers are not constants of nature. Drepper's are for a Pentium M, CMU's for Haswell, and every CPU differs. Use them to reason about *ratios* (a DRAM access costs tens to hundreds of L1 hits), and measure your own machine before quoting absolute cycles.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Transcoders and cross-layer transcoders
md: Collapsing chains is not free. If the real model really runs a mutually reinforcing loop (the paper sees Copenhagen and Denmark features exciting each other with per-layer transcoders), a CLT can hide it. Simpler graphs can mean less faithful graphs.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: IPS fixes the examination part of the bias, not click noise. If users sometimes click irrelevant results, those clicks are also upweighted. Joachims et al. show that, as long as relevant results are clicked more often than irrelevant ones, this bias is order preserving: with enough data the best ranking stays the same, but the estimates are no longer exactly relevance.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Image search with CLIP, the modality gap, and where it fails
md: Do not compare scores across modalities with one threshold. Image-image cosines and text-image cosines come from different regions of the space, so a cutoff tuned for text queries will not transfer to image queries, and a mixed index of image and text vectors will tend to rank same-modality items together.

courseTitle: Columnar storage and vectorized execution
lessonTitle: Arrow in memory: buffers, validity bitmaps and offsets
md: Arrow is not a file format for long-term storage like Parquet. Arrow data is laid out for fast random access and computation and is normally uncompressed in memory (the IPC format allows only optional LZ4 or ZSTD buffer compression); Parquet is encoded and compressed for small size on disk. A typical pipeline reads Parquet and decodes it into Arrow-style (or engine-specific) column vectors.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization
md: Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: A computer-use agent is an ordinary agent loop where the tool is "the computer" and the observation is a screenshot. The model proposes actions in screenshot pixel coordinates; the harness executes them, and is the only place you can enforce scaling, safety and verification.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: loom only sees what goes through loom types. A `std::sync::Mutex` or a third-party lock inside your code still runs, but loom cannot schedule around it, so executions that are possible in reality are silently not modeled. Libraries you depend on need loom support too for full coverage.

courseTitle: Consistency models and one-step diffusion
lessonTitle: Self-consistency: every point on a trajectory maps to its origin
md: A consistency model is not a one-step denoiser. A network trained with plain regression to $x_0$ from $x_T$ learns the conditional mean, which is blurry for images and collapses in the toy. The consistency function is a deterministic map along ODE trajectories, so its outputs keep the full data spread.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: Eventual consistency, session guarantees and real systems
md: CAP, in Gilbert and Lynch's proof, is about a single linearizable register: during a network partition you cannot have both linearizability and a response from every non-failing node. Without a partition you can have both. Kleppmann argues that precise model names beat CP and AP labels.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction: hard filters, then soft scoring
lessonTitle: Must-haves and nice-to-haves need different machinery
md: Hard constraints decide **who is in**; soft constraints decide **the order**. Never let a preference buy its way past a requirement, and never let a preference silently remove someone.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Arc consistency: AC-3 prunes domains before guessing
md: Search guesses; propagation deduces. Every modern CP solver alternates: make one decision, propagate to a fixpoint, and backtrack only when some domain becomes empty.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: The filters object and its four update operations
md: Model the state as a fixed schema where every slot is present and null means unconstrained. Each turn applies one of a few explicit operations per slot, and carryover is the default.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Plausible is not faithful: the biasing-feature test
md: Misconception: "if every step of the CoT is correct, the CoT explains the answer." Turpin et al. found unfaithful CoTs with no obvious errors. Checking that reasoning is *valid* tests plausibility. Only a counterfactual (change an input the CoT ignores and see if the answer moves) tests faithfulness.

courseTitle: CPU and GPU co-scheduling: streams, pinned memory and overlap
lessonTitle: Streams, the default stream trap, and events
md: Three independent facts, often confused. A stream gives you **ordering** (and is always sequential inside itself). Separate streams give you **permission** to overlap. The hardware (`asyncEngineCount`, concurrent kernel support, free SMs) decides whether overlap actually **happens**. Two streams on a one-copy-engine GPU will still serialize their two transfers against each other.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Training a reranker: pointwise, pairwise, listwise and hard negatives
md: Hard negative mining has a trap: MS MARCO labels about one relevant passage per query, so many top-ranked unlabeled passages are actually relevant. Training to push them down teaches the model wrong lessons. mine_hard_negatives offers margins and a max_score cap partly to skip such false negatives.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: From MMA atoms to TiledMMA and TiledCopy
md: Shared memory layout matters as much as thread layout. The sgemm_2 tutorial pads its shared memory layouts (stride bM + 1) to avoid bank conflicts, and Hopper TMA can write swizzled layouts for the same reason. A layout that is correct can still be slow.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Worked example: what a CXL access costs
md: Do not assume every CXL device behaves like Pond's model. Sun et al. measured three real devices: one had ld latency only 35% longer than a remote-socket DDR5 node, while the other two were about 2x and 3x longer. Their bandwidth efficiency also differed widely by controller. Emulating CXL with a remote NUMA socket, as early research did, can mislead in both directions.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Knobs, failure modes, and what came after DoReMi
md: Weights depend on the setup that produced them. Domain weights are measured in tokens, so they shift with the **tokenizer** (the paper used a 256k SentencePiece vocabulary; the repo warns this changes mixtures). They also depend on the **training budget**: weights moved fast in the first 50k steps, so a shorter run may want a different mix. Rerun DoReMi in your own setup rather than copying published weights.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: Worked example: binary search over animation keyframes
md: Measure what the hot path *reads repeatedly*. Splitting the search key from its payload shrinks the working set the loop revisits, which often matters more than the miss count of a single call.

courseTitle: Deterministic simulation testing: replayable chaos in distributed code
lessonTitle: Making rare states common: faults, BUGGIFY and swarm testing
md: To find rare bugs, maximize the *diversity* of runs, not the intensity of each one. Random per-run choices of faults, features and buggify sites cover far more distinct states than one heavily tuned configuration.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why parallel decoding breaks, and how to make it fast
md: Diffusion decoding uses fewer sequential passes but more total compute per answer. It wins wall-clock time only when each pass is memory-bound (small batches, interactive latency). Caching and confidence thresholds exist to shrink the compute overhead without giving back the parallelism.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: Why DPO skips the reward model and the RL loop
md: DPO is not "RLHF without a reward". It fits the same Bradley-Terry reward model, just parameterized through the policy. It also inherits the KL objective's $\beta$. What it removes is the separate reward network and on-policy sampling during training.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Why a live data migration needs four careful phases
md: Turning on dual writes does not make the stores identical. It only covers objects written *after* the switch. Objects that are never updated again stay only in the old store until the backfill copies them.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Why run your tracing logic inside the kernel
md: eBPF lets you run your own logic at the moment an event happens, inside the kernel, with a load-time proof that it cannot crash or hang the machine. bpftrace makes that a one-liner: probe, optional filter, action, and maps that summarize in the kernel.

courseTitle: Edge AI: quantization, pruning and small models for devices
lessonTitle: Fewer operations and fewer weights, then shipping it
md: Pruning does not automatically make a model smaller or faster. The LiteRT docs state that pruned models are the same size on disk and have the same latency; they only compress better. You get size savings from a sparse format or compression, and speed only from kernels or hardware that skip zeros. With 8-bit values plus 8-bit gaps, sparse storage only wins once more than half the weights are zero.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Budget forcing, effort levels and hard caps at inference
md: A small output-token cap is not a cheap way to get short reasoning. The model does not know about the cap, so it can be cut off mid-thought, and you pay for the thinking tokens with nothing to show. Use the effort or budget control that the model was trained to respond to.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Neural NILM, seq2point, and the unseen-house problem
md: Every NILM method injects prior knowledge to resolve an unidentifiable sum. Hart hand-designs it (step signatures), FHMMs encode it as state machines, and neural nets learn it from sub-metered houses. The test that matters is a house the model never saw.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Job titles: taxonomies, seniority and embeddings
md: General-purpose embedding models do not know your abbreviations (`SWE`, `SDET`, `RN`) and blur words that share context (`sales engineer` vs `software engineer`). Expand abbreviations before embedding, match against many alternate titles rather than one label, and keep an *unknown* outcome instead of forcing the nearest code.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: The winner's curse: why the best public score is too high
md: The maximum of many noisy scores is biased upward. Selecting a system on a query set uses up that set: its score for the winner is no longer an unbiased estimate. The bias grows with the number of systems tried (roughly like sqrt(ln N)) and shrinks with more queries (like 1/sqrt(n)).

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Contamination: when test queries leak into training data
md: Putting it together: split by query cluster and time, tune on dev, read a sealed and rotating test set rarely, report paired bootstrap CIs, correct for every comparison you run, and check for contamination with fresh queries the model could not have seen.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: FedAvg exactly, worked on three clients over two rounds
md: A common misreading is that FedAvg averages the clients' answers. It averages their **parameters**. In this problem the sample-weighted average of the three local optima is 1.667 and the plain average is 2.0, while the true optimum is 2.3. Averaging models that have fully solved their own problems gives the wrong model.

courseTitle: Filtered ANN with ACORN: predicate subgraph traversal
lessonTitle: ACORN-gamma: expand every neighbor list by gamma
md: Misconception: "just raise M in HNSW". The paper notes that Qdrant's earlier densification idea did this, but $M$ also sets HNSW's level multiplier $m_L = 1/\ln M$, so raising it flattens the hierarchy, and HNSW is sensitive to its number of levels. ACORN keeps $M$ (and therefore $m_L$ and the level structure) fixed and expands the lists by $\gamma$ instead.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: Online softmax: exact attention one block at a time
md: Online softmax is exact. The running max is only for numerical safety (keeping $e^x$ from overflowing); any consistent reference point gives the same $O/l$. Every FlashAttention version computes the same math; they differ only in how the work is mapped onto the hardware.

courseTitle: FlashInfer: an attention engine for LLM serving
lessonTitle: Tile sizes, GQA head fusion and JIT attention variants
md: FlashInfer = one block-sparse view of every KV layout, attention states merged with $\oplus$ so work can be split and composed freely, a per-step plan that balances skewed lengths while staying CUDA-graph friendly, and a JIT template so new variants get fused kernels instead of new libraries.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: NVFP4: 16-value blocks, E4M3 scales and a tensor scale
md: In NVFP4 the amax of every 16-value block is encoded at close to FP8 precision (the block scale is E4M3), which is at least 1/16 = 6.25% of all values. MXFP4 stores every value, the amax included, at FP4 precision behind a power-of-two scale.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Filling the Wagner-Fischer table cell by cell
md: The table gives one number, but several different edit sequences can tie for the minimum. The traceback picks one of them. Do not read a single alignment as *the* explanation of how two strings differ.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: The Astrometry.net quad code, computed step by step
md: Invariant does not mean mirror-proof. Some cameras and optical paths flip the image. Astrometry.net's code-flip helper swaps each (x, y) pair, and the solver defaults to trying both parities. Groth's triangle method instead records whether vertices run clockwise and accepts either sense.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Radius search: cover with cells, then check exact distance
md: `WHERE ST_Distance(a, b) < 500` gives the right answer but cannot use the spatial index, so it scans every row. The PostGIS docs pair them deliberately: use `ST_DWithin` to limit the search with the index, then `ST_Distance` only for sorting the few survivors.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Why frameworks do not call cudaMalloc for every tensor
md: Misconception: "nvidia-smi shows 20 GB used, so my tensors use 20 GB." It shows reserved memory plus the CUDA context. Compare `memory_allocated()` with `memory_reserved()` before hunting for a leak.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: From registers to HBM: the GPU memory map
md: **Local memory is not local to the chip.** The word refers to scope (one thread), not location. Spilled registers, large per-thread arrays and arrays indexed with values the compiler cannot resolve at compile time all go to local memory, which has the latency and bandwidth of global memory.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: Case study: one matrix transpose, three kernels
md: The NVIDIA post's conclusion: coalescing global memory accesses is by far the most critical step. Use shared memory to turn strided global access into coalesced access, then check the shared access for bank conflicts.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: How profiling perturbs what it measures
md: Decide which question you are asking before you choose the flags. Isolated-kernel analysis wants the defaults: locked clocks, flushed caches, serialized launches. System-representative behavior wants `--replay-mode application --clock-control none --cache-control none`. Mixing the two across runs produces numbers that disagree for reasons that have nothing to do with your code.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: From chunks to an entity graph with LLM extraction
md: Entity matching is exact string matching (the paper says so explicitly). If one chunk says "Quillfern Labs" and another says "Quillfern", you get two nodes. The paper notes GraphRAG is fairly resilient because such duplicates usually end up in the same community, but in practice prompt tuning or an entity-resolution pass matters.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Lighter graph RAG: FastGraphRAG, LightRAG, HippoRAG
md: Graph RAG variants differ in where they spend LLM calls: GraphRAG spends heavily at indexing (extraction, summaries, reports) and on map calls per global query; FastGraphRAG cuts extraction; LightRAG drops communities; HippoRAG drops summaries and lets PPR do the multi-hop work.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: What a GTFS Schedule zip contains and how its tables join
md: A stop can appear twice in one trip, for example on a loop route where the bus starts and ends at the same stop. That is why `stop_sequence`, not `stop_id`, identifies a row of a trip. Code that keys stop times by `stop_id` alone silently overwrites one visit with the other.

courseTitle: Hardware performance counters: measuring why code is slow
lessonTitle: perf stat: counting, multiplexing and scaled estimates
md: A percentage in parentheses after a `perf stat` line, like `(74.98%)`, means that event ran only that fraction of the time and was scaled. Treat such numbers as estimates, and be most suspicious when the workload has phases.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Design rule of thumb from published ablations: keep roughly 8% to 12% of layers as global attention, spread them evenly, start with an SSM layer, and expect long-context KV savings close to (attention layers in the Transformer you replace) / (attention layers you keep), at equal KV heads: 32 / 4 = 8x for Nemotron-H-8B vs Nemotron-T-8B, not 52 / 4 = 13x.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Why change detection must align images first
md: Alignment comes before differencing, always. Without it, the change mask mostly measures camera motion, concentrated on every edge in the image.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Two shared rings: SQEs, CQEs, head and tail
md: If the tail update becomes visible before the SQE fields, the kernel can read a half-written request (say, the right opcode with a stale fd). This is a real bug class in hand-rolled ring code. liburing does the barriers for you, which is the main reason to use it even if you want raw control elsewhere.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
md: mimalloc replaces a per-thread cache with ownership: the thread that owns a page allocates and frees into it with plain loads and stores, and everyone else uses a per-page atomic list that the owner drains in batches.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
md: Elle never solves for a transaction order. It designs the workload so reads expose the version order, then turns the history into a dependency graph and looks for cycles. A cycle is a concrete, explainable counterexample, and its edge types name the anomaly.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: The per-packet budget: why the kernel path runs out of cycles
md: Kernel bypass means the **device driver lives in your process**. Data moves between device and application memory by DMA, the application learns about it by polling memory, and nothing on the per-packet or per-I/O path enters the kernel.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Why chains of elementwise ops are memory bound
md: Misconception: "the GPU is slow at GELU because tanh is expensive". Profile first. A standalone GELU kernel on a large tensor is limited by the read and the write of the tensor, not by tanh.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: The distillation loss and why it is scaled by T squared
md: Soft gradient = (q - p) / T, which shrinks like 1 over T squared. Multiply the soft loss by T squared so temperature changes what is matched without changing how much it counts.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Quantizing keys per channel and values per token (KIVI)
md: Keys: quantize per channel, because outliers live in fixed channels. Values: quantize per token, because the output mixes value rows. Keep the most recent tokens in full precision until a group is complete.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
md: Offloading does not make attention read from CPU memory. In reuse offloading, blocks are copied back into GPU blocks before the attention kernel runs; the kernel only ever sees HBM. What offloading buys is skipping the *prefill compute* that would otherwise recreate those blocks.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
md: Happened-before means *information could have flowed* from a to b through process order and messages. It is a partial order: many pairs of events are simply concurrent, and no clock reading can change that.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Why one vector per document leaves accuracy behind
md: Late interaction = independent encoding (so documents are precomputed) + token-level matching at query time (so fine-grained evidence is not averaged away into one vector).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
md: Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
md: A learned index does not return approximate answers. It finds exactly the same record a B-tree would. Only the *path* to the record is approximate; the final local search makes the answer exact.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Why learn sparse vectors instead of dense ones
md: A learned sparse vector is still a bag of weighted terms, so it can live in a normal inverted index. The transformer only decides *which* terms get *how much* weight, including terms absent from the text.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaMART: boosted trees that fit the lambdas
md: Simplified for teaching: one query and a stump with least-squares splits, as in Burges's description. LightGBM and XGBoost grow deeper trees from millions of rows and choose splits with a gain computed from summed gradients and hessians, and LightGBM also rescales the pushes per query when lambdarank_norm is on. The mechanism, fitting trees to lambdas, is the same.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Gated DeltaNet: targeted writes plus fast forgetting
md: Gated DeltaNet's one-line change: decay first with a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then do a delta-rule write with $\beta_t$. $\alpha_t\to0$ clears memory at a context switch; $\alpha_t\to1$ keeps it and lets the delta rule edit single associations.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: BLEU, ROUGE and BERTScore, and where they fail
md: Overlap metrics measure closeness to a reference, not correctness. A fluent answer with one wrong fact can outscore a correct paraphrase. They also penalize outputs that are better than, but different from, the reference, which is common once a strong LLM writes the outputs.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Measuring a guard, and why no guard is complete
md: Layers multiply only if their failures are independent. Two guards that miss 20% and 30% of attacks miss 6% together if independent, but an adaptive attacker searches for inputs that fool both at once. Assume some attacks get through, and limit what a successful one can do: least privilege, human approval, monitoring and incident response.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: "No mutex in the code" does not make an algorithm lock-free. If one stalled thread can prevent all others from completing, it is blocking, even if it only uses atomic instructions. Michael and Scott call out published queues that are "lock-free but not non-blocking" for exactly this reason, and Vyukov says the same of their own bounded queue (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Freeing nodes safely: hazard pointers and epochs
md: Lock-free data structures are two problems: the CAS protocol that keeps the structure consistent, and the reclamation scheme that keeps removed nodes alive until no thread can still be reading them. Get both right, or use a library that has.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Why models break past their trained length
md: RoPE is called a relative encoding, so it is tempting to think it should extrapolate for free. It does not: dimensions whose wavelength exceeds the training length never wrap, so in practice they leak absolute position, and new positions mean new, unseen angles.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
md: Overlap condition: $c \ge F/B$. Fast links (NVLink, TPU ICI) need blocks of about 1K tokens; slow links need tens of thousands. Causal masks require striping or zigzag chunk assignment, or the busiest rank sets the pace.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Spending compute at test time: more loops, early exits, shared caches
md: Per-token early exit saves FLOPs per token, but in batched serving tokens that exit early may sit idle waiting for others. Relaxed Recursive Transformers (Bae et al. 2024) propose **continuous depth-wise batching**, scheduling new work into slots freed by early exits; their simulation estimates 2 to 3x throughput, not a measured deployment.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: Low scores on forget benchmarks show suppressed outputs, not erased knowledge. Small fine-tunes, probes and even 4-bit quantization can bring "forgotten" knowledge back, because approximate unlearning moves the weights only slightly.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
md: Misconception: more TP is a free way to save memory. Per-GPU TP traffic stays near 8bsh per layer however large t gets, every GEMM gets t times smaller (lower GPU efficiency), and once t exceeds the GPUs in one server the all-reduces leave NVLink for the much slower network. Narayanan et al.'s Takeaway 1: use TP up to the server size (8 on DGX A100), then PP across servers.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Size classes: buying speed with internal waste
md: `sizeof` is not what you pay. With a million 130-byte records you might budget 124 MiB, but jemalloc hands out 160 bytes each (153 MiB) and a power-of-two allocator 256 (244 MiB). Measure with `malloc_usable_size` or allocator stats, not by multiplying `sizeof`.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Acquire and release: publishing data across threads
md: There is no "acquire store" or "release load". Release only affects stores and Acquire only affects loads; SeqCst cannot create them either. A Release store and a Release store never synchronize with each other.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
md: EBR pays per operation, not per node, and needs no per-node announcement. In exchange, a single thread stalled while pinned blocks all reclamation, so garbage is unbounded.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
md: A triplet only produces gradient when the negative is inside d(a,p) + m. Mining decides which of those active triplets you spend compute on.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Warm caches in the benchmark, cold caches in production
md: A microbenchmark's working set and access pattern are part of the experiment. Report them next to the time, and sweep the size if the code's data can be large.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Token-in-token-out: train on the tokens you actually sampled
md: `role_content_only` is marked high risk. A tool-calling turn often has empty visible text, so two turns that called different tools can match. The stored prefix then wins, and the trainer keeps a history showing a call the agent never made, silently.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Learned indexes: a model that predicts where a key lives
md: Model execution must be nearly free. The paper's first attempt ran a 2-layer, 32-neuron net through TensorFlow from Python: about 80,000 ns per prediction, versus about 300 ns for a whole B-tree traversal. Their Learning Index Framework instead extracts the trained weights and generates small C++ index code, never calling TensorFlow at lookup time.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: MLA in production: kernels, prefill, parallelism, results
md: Do not credit MLA with every DeepSeek-V2 headline. Against DeepSeek 67B, V2 reports a 93.3% smaller KV cache and 5.76x maximum generation throughput (over 50K tokens per second on one 8-GPU H800 node), but the deployed system also used FP8 weights, KV cache quantization to about 6 bits per element, and a sparse MoE. The 42.5% training cost saving comes from MoE, not MLA.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Why one phrasing of a question misses relevant documents
md: Retrieval quality depends on the exact words of the query. Multi-query retrieval treats the user's wording as one sample from many possible phrasings and retrieves with several samples instead of betting on one.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: Bi-encoder, late interaction, cross-encoder: where the cost goes
md: Precompute versus interact. The more of the query-document comparison happens at query time, the more accurate and the more expensive the scorer. Bi-encoders and late interaction can serve as first stages over an index; cross-encoders only fit on short candidate lists.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: Reusing the extra heads to decode faster
md: MTP gives two separate benefits: a training signal that can make the main model better, and heads that can draft tokens for exact, faster greedy decoding. You can use the first without the second by discarding the heads.

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Scaling Muon to LLMs, distributing it, and choosing an optimizer
md: Do not judge an optimizer by a single untuned comparison. The Muon post argues that most papers claiming to beat AdamW used undertuned baselines, and proposes competitive benchmarks (like the NanoGPT speedrun record, where anyone can revert to AdamW) as the standard of evidence.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
md: A lock is two things at once: mutual exclusion (one atomic read-modify-write decides a single winner) and visibility (Acquire on lock, Release on unlock, so each unlock happens-before the next lock).

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Why a database keeps old copies of rows
md: MVCC is not the same as no locking. Two transactions that update the *same* row still conflict: the second one waits for the first to commit or roll back. MVCC only stops readers and writers from blocking each other.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
md: SSI = snapshot isolation plus non-blocking tracking of rw edges. It aborts a transaction in any dangerous structure, so every committed set is serializable; the application's job is to retry on 40001.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
md: Theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. A sparse attention method is only fast if the GPU reads fewer bytes in contiguous chunks during every phase (training, prefill, decode), and it only keeps quality if the model is trained with the sparsity.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: PDQ, learned copy detectors and building a real pipeline
md: Global hashes, PDQ included, do poorly when one image is a **crop** of another; the PDQ document lists deep crops as out of scope. ImageHash's documentation shows how fast aHash degrades with rotation on its test image: 2 bits at 1 degree, 11 at 6 degrees, 21 at 26 degrees. Large borders, overlaid text and memes also defeat them.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Why some memory is farther away than other memory
md: NUMA means the cost of a cache miss depends on which node holds the page. Keep each thread's data on the node where the thread runs.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
md: Locality needs both halves: pages on the right node, and threads that stay there. Pin, or let NUMA balancing migrate pages, and verify placement with numa_maps rather than allocation counters.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
md: Raising the confidence threshold does not always raise precision. It only helps if the boxes it removes are mostly false positives. A confidently wrong box, like B3 at 0.75, survives every threshold that keeps it.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
md: Write data under fresh names, then commit a reference atomically. Use a create-if-absent or compare-and-swap on the commit point so that exactly one writer can ever extend the history.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Traces: spans, context propagation, and what sampling throws away
md: A trace is kept or dropped as a whole, and the decision is made by whoever starts it. Head sampling trades away rare events; tail sampling buys them back with buffering and stateful collectors. Never read a trace count as a request count.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Adding layout: from LayoutLM boxes to OCR-free Donut
md: Forgetting to normalize is a classic bug. Raw pixel coordinates from a 1700 x 2200 scan exceed the 1024-entry position tables and crash with an index error, or, if clipped, silently collapse the lower part of the page onto the same embedding.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: Targets, PUBLIC vs PRIVATE, and why links fail
md: Declare every real dependency on the target that uses it, with the narrowest correct scope: PRIVATE if only the .cpp files use it, PUBLIC if your headers expose it, INTERFACE if only your headers do. CMake then derives include paths, definitions and link order for you.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
md: Do not add `@pytest.mark.flaky` or `xfail` to a test your PR broke. Maintainers read that as hiding a failure. If you believe a failure is pre-existing flakiness, show evidence: the same test failing on `main` or on other PRs, or a seed that reproduces it without your change.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: Review by email: patch versions and trailer tags
md: You may not add a Reviewed-by, Tested-by or Acked-by tag for someone just because they said nice things. The kernel guide says these need the named person's explicit permission; only Cc:, Reported-by: and Suggested-by: can be added with implicit permission.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
md: Before using an AI tool on a contribution, find the project's policy (CONTRIBUTING, developer docs, or the docs on patch submission). Then: never submit what you cannot explain, disclose as the project asks, and never let a tool add your sign-off.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Pushing rewritten history: --force-with-lease and its limits
md: `--force-with-lease` says "overwrite only if the remote is still what I last fetched". Add `--force-if-includes` so a fetch alone does not count as having seen the remote's commits.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Inbound licensing: inbound=outbound and contributor agreements
md: The most common CLA failure is an email mismatch: the commits use a personal or unregistered address while the agreement (or the employer's group) lists another. Fix the author email and rewrite the commits, not the agreement.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? t-tests, U tests and p-values
md: Significant is not the same as large. benchstat's docs stress that with enough low-noise data even very small changes become significant. Report the size of the change and its spread, and use the test only to answer "is this more than noise?"

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: What a maintainer needs: a failure they can run themselves
md: A bug report's first job is to let the maintainer make the failure happen themselves. Everything else in the report (description, guesses about the cause) comes second.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Intermittent bugs, seeds, and environment differences
md: A flaky repro is not done until it fails every time or you know its failure rate. Pin seeds and inputs, report versions, and repeat runs enough times that a PASS means something.

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Self-review the diff, then use drafts to signal readiness
md: Self-review first, then mark ready. A reviewable PR is focused, explained, clean, and honestly labeled as draft or ready.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, and when caching pays
md: Longest-prefix-first can starve a request whose prefix is never cached, since others keep jumping ahead. The SGLang paper says so and leaves fair scheduling as future work.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: Broken stacks: frame pointers, DWARF, LBR and symbols
md: Missing callers, a detached tower over [unknown], or hex instead of names are not hot spots. They are profiler blind spots. Fix frame pointers or symbols before you trust the picture.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Alignment: which addresses a type is allowed to start at
md: "x86 handles misaligned loads, so alignment does not matter" is a common misconception. In C the rule is in the language, not just the CPU: converting a pointer to a type whose alignment the address does not satisfy is **undefined behavior** (C11 6.3.2.3p7). The optimizer may assume every `int *` is 4-aligned, whatever the CPU tolerates.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
md: OKS is averaged per object over *labeled* keypoints, so a person with only 4 labeled points counts as much as one with 17. Also, persons too small to have keypoint labels are not evaluated, and at most 20 detections per image are scored. Comparing OKS numbers across datasets with different skeletons or sigmas is meaningless.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Query planners: choosing a strategy by selectivity
md: No single plan wins everywhere. Broad filters favor graph search with the filter applied during or after it; restrictive filters favor brute force over an allow list; the middle is where graphs fragment and filter-aware indexes like ACORN and Filtered-DiskANN earn their keep. The deciding input is the estimated number of matches.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: Grading the answer versus grading every step
md: An ORM gets one label per solution and must discover where errors are. A PRM is told where the first error is. That extra information is why PRMs rank solutions better on hard problems, and why they can reject right answers reached by wrong reasoning.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Anatomy of a context switch, step by step
md: Register save and restore is the same for every switch. The difference between a thread switch and a process switch is the address space: if `next` shares `prev`'s memory, the page table stays loaded and the TLB stays valid.

courseTitle: Automatic prompt optimization: APE, OPRO and DSPy
lessonTitle: Why hand-tuned prompts are brittle
md: Misconception: "a prompt that works is a good prompt". A hand-tuned prompt is fitted to one model, one task and the handful of examples you looked at. Change the model, the data or even the separator characters and the ranking of prompts can change.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
md: Any structural comparison in this field is after optimal superposition. A reported RMSD of 1.4 Angstrom always means 1.4 after Kabsch alignment; the unaligned number is meaningless because it depends on where the coordinates happen to be written down.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Why the query the user typed is rarely the query to send
md: The retriever only sees what you send it. Rewriting changes *which* query is sent; decomposition changes *how many* queries are sent and in what order. Both are bets that a better query beats a better index.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: The unbiased estimator and its O(1/sqrt(D)) error
md: Unbiased does not mean accurate on each pair. It means the errors average out to zero instead of pushing every estimate the same way. Per-pair accuracy comes from concentration: the 1/sqrt(D) shrinkage.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
md: RAG splits knowledge in two: the index decides **what facts are available**, the LLM decides **how they are read and phrased**. Every quality problem in this course is a failure of one of these two halves, or of the hand-off between them.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
md: A raw click count rewards documents for having been ranked high in the past, which feeds back into ranking them high again. Correcting this (for example the propensity weighting of Joachims, Swaminathan and Schnabel 2017) is a topic of its own; at minimum, normalize clicks by impressions and record the position each impression was shown at.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Three runs, seven verdicts: when metrics disagree
md: Disagreement between metrics is information, not noise. If binary metrics and exponential nDCG disagree, your system is trading coverage of relevant documents against putting the very best one first. Report at least one metric of each kind and say which user you care about.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
md: In practice: register big pools on huge pages, keep the number of connected QPs bounded (share, or use UD for fan-out), batch posts behind one doorbell, inline small payloads, signal selectively, avoid hot atomics, and handle error completions by resetting or recreating the connection.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Delta-encoded state and choosing the transport
md: Bandwidth is set by what changes, how it is encoded, and how often you send it. Latency under loss is set by the transport: an ordered stream turns one lost packet into a stall for every later update.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
md: A gap between a random-split number and a temporal-split number is not a bug in either; they measure different tasks. Only the temporal one resembles what the system will face, so compare models on that.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: Aggregation and sorting: running state, hash tables and spills
md: Aggregation keeps a small state per group. Hashing finds the state with a table (memory grows with groups); sorting brings each group together so one state suffices (needs ordered input). Sort and hash nodes both spill to disk when they exceed their memory limit.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Concurrent writes, conflict resolution and what quorums do not promise
md: Pick the knobs by the question each one answers: **N** sets how many copies survive, **W** how many machines must hold a write before "ok", **R** how many you ask on a read, and **the conflict rule** decides what happens when copies disagree. Real configs: Dynamo's common (3, 2, 2); R = 1, W = N for read-heavy catalogs; Cassandra QUORUM with QUORUM.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: One RL step is five workloads on two kinds of engine
md: Rollout is the bottleneck. FLOPs are dominated by training, but wall-clock time is dominated by sequential decoding. Most RL infrastructure ideas (fast inference engines, placement, resharding, asynchrony, partial rollouts) are ways to make generation faster or to keep the other GPUs busy while it runs.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: The roofline: attainable FLOP/s versus intensity
md: The ridge point tells you how hard the machine is to feed. The paper notes that a ridge far to the right means only kernels with very high intensity can reach peak. From the V100 (138.9) to the H100 in BF16 (295.4), the ridge more than doubled.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: Trigger, proximate cause, contributing factors, action items
md: The one thing to keep: triage narrows, mitigation buys time, and the postmortem is where the next incident gets cheaper. Each of the three uses a different artifact: the dependency graph and the distributions for narrowing, a rehearsed rollback or kill switch for mitigating, and a list of named conditions with owners for not doing it again.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: When score fusion beats RRF
md: Tuning RRF is not free robustness. Bruch et al. found that per-list constants tuned in-domain generalized poorly out-of-domain (HotpotQA fell from 0.675 to 0.621), while a convex combination's single α transferred well. If you tune, validate on traffic that looks like production.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
md: A CPU only ever runs tasks from its own local DSQ. Everything else (global DSQ, custom DSQs, BPF maps) is staging. The pick order is local, then global, then `ops.dispatch()`.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
md: The search policy is a better policy than the network that guided it. Training the network to imitate it is **policy improvement by imitation**. No human labels are used, but new information does enter the loop: from look-ahead, and from the game rules that score every finished game.

courseTitle: Semantic caching and prompt compression
lessonTitle: Choosing the threshold: hit rate against false hits
md: Do not copy a threshold from a tutorial or a library default. Collect a few hundred real pairs from your traffic, label whether the cached answer would be correct, and pick the threshold from that data and your cost of a wrong answer. Re-check whenever you change the embedding model, since similarity scales differ between models.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Cache-aware scheduling: queue order sets the hit rate
md: Greedy longest-prefix-first can **starve** a request whose prefix is never cached: requests that hit keep jumping ahead of it. The paper says so directly and leaves fair cache-aware scheduling as future work. Watch tail latency if you enable `lpm`.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: A*: steering the search with a lower bound
md: A* is Dijkstra with key g + h. Never overestimate (admissible) and you keep optimality; satisfy the triangle inequality (consistent) and each node is settled once. The closer h is to the true remaining cost, the fewer nodes settle.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: IIR filters, zero-phase filtering and real sensor data
md: Pick the filter by the job: moving average to smooth in time, windowed-sinc FIR (firwin) for clean band separation with linear phase, Butterworth IIR (as SOS) for a cheap sharp cutoff. Offline, filter forward and backward to cancel the delay.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Arm Neon and SVE: fixed width versus length agnostic
md: Neon is fixed 128-bit SIMD. SVE is vector-length agnostic: 128 to 2048 bits (a power of two), chosen by the chip. Predicates from whilelt make the tail just another iteration, so one binary scales across vector lengths.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Three modules, one loop: how slime is laid out
md: slime is a thin layer: Ray places the workers, SGLang generates, Megatron trains, and slime owns the glue in between (the Data Buffer, the rollout function and weight sync). Most behavior you might want to change is a command-line flag or a function path, not a fork.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Fully async rollout and the price of staleness
md: Async in slime means: same train.py, different rollout function, separate GPU pools. You trade a bounded amount of policy staleness for not waiting on the slowest trajectory.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
md: Judge an SAE by sparsity (L0), reconstruction (FVU) and downstream loss together, then verify interpretations causally. Steering by clamping a latent equals adding $(c - f_i)$ times its decoder direction while keeping the SAE error.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Ordinary kriging: solving for the best weights
md: Negative weights mean an ordinary kriging estimate can fall outside the range of the readings. That can be right for a smooth field with a peak between sensors, but for quantities that must stay positive (rainfall, concentrations) check for negative predictions.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: How many tokens per round, and what speedup to expect
md: Speedup is not tokens per pass. A draft that is accurate but slow (high alpha, high c) can lose to a weaker but nearly free one. Leviathan et al. found drafts about two orders of magnitude smaller than the target usually balanced alpha and c best.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Long audio, streaming and hallucinations in production
md: Silence is where a language-model decoder is least constrained by audio. Short clips are padded to 30 s, long pauses leave long stretches of nothing, and the decoder can fill them with plausible web-caption text. The repetition and confidence checks do not catch a fluent, confident invented sentence.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: TLB reach, huge pages and shootdowns
md: Huge pages are not free. The THP documentation warns that a process that maps a large region but touches one byte can get a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, and allocating a huge page needs 2 MiB of *physically contiguous* memory, which may require compaction. That is why `madvise` mode exists.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Two clocks: why sensor readings arrive out of order
md: Window by **event time** (when the device measured) whenever the result should describe the physical world. Processing time describes your pipeline, not your sensor: a network hiccup would change a temperature average.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Downsampling, retention and exactly-once vs at-least-once
md: Misconception: "QoS 2 at the device makes the pipeline exactly-once". MQTT QoS covers one hop. The bridge, Kafka producer, stream job and sink each need their own guarantee, and a single at-least-once hop reintroduces duplicates.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Training recipe, quadratic cost and what changed since 2017
md: "Transformer" does not mean "GPT". The 2017 model is an encoder-decoder for translation. Decoder-only language models keep only its masked self-attention stack; encoder-only models keep only the unmasked encoder.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Next-token prediction: turning raw text into training examples
md: Training is **teacher forcing on every position in parallel**: the true previous tokens are always the context, and all $B \times T$ predictions are scored in one pass. Generation is the opposite, one token at a time feeding its own outputs back in.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
md: Training scores all positions in parallel with teacher forcing; generation is a sequential loop over the same network that samples from the last position's distribution, shaped by temperature and top-k.

courseTitle: Calculus and gradients: from slopes to backpropagation
lessonTitle: Gradient descent: walking downhill and choosing the step size
md: A rising loss does not always mean a bug in your gradients. With a correct gradient, too large a learning rate alone makes training diverge, as $\eta = 0.35$ did here. Lowering $\eta$ is the first thing to try.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
md: pipefail meets SIGPIPE: with pipefail on, `yes | head -n 1` has status 141, because yes was killed when head exited. `seq 1 3 | head -n 1` returns 0 only because all its output fit in the pipe before head quit. Under `set -e`, a producer piped into `head` can end the script on large inputs; test such pipelines at realistic sizes.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Inside a GPU: many small cores fed by one big memory
md: More cores does not mean every program runs faster. If each operation reads a lot of data and does little math per byte, the SMs wait on HBM no matter how many there are. The next lesson turns this into a number.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: From hello.c to a running process
md: A **program** is a file of bytes on disk. A **process** is a running instance of it: its own memory (code, data, heap, stack), its own register values, and OS bookkeeping such as open files. One program can be running as many processes at once.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: The OS in charge: system calls and sharing the CPU
md: The OS is not running alongside your program; it runs only when something hands it the CPU: a system call (the program asks), an exception (the program did something illegal), or an interrupt (hardware such as the timer or the disk demands attention).

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
md: RLHF does not maximize reward. It maximizes reward minus beta times the KL from the SFT model, and beta sets how far the model may move to chase the reward model.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: TF-IDF: weighting by frequency and rarity
md: The base of the log in idf does not change the ranking: switching from log10 to ln multiplies every idf by the same constant (about 2.303), so every score scales equally. What does matter is the shape, for example whether tf is raw or sublinear.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Arrays, pointer arithmetic and strings
md: Off by one is the classic C bug: `for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) a[i] = 0;` writes a[n], one element past the end. The loop condition for an n-element array is `i < n`. Neither the compiler nor the CPU checks array bounds for you.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Moves, Copy and clone: why let s2 = s1 kills s1
md: A move is not a deep copy and not a pointer trick at run time. It is a shallow copy of the value's bytes **plus** a compile-time rule that the source is dead. The heap block never moves.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: A vector is a list of numbers and an arrow at the same time
md: A vector is an ordered list of $n$ numbers and also an arrow in $n$-dimensional space. Addition and scaling act component by component; the norm is the arrow's length.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: Where it shows up: linear layers, batches and attention scores
md: Linear layers are batched dot products ($XW^\top + b$). Attention scores are dot products between queries and keys ($QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k}$). Similarity search is a matrix-vector product. Vectors, dot products and matrix multiplication cover all three.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
md: Choose capacity and regularization by **validation** error, keep the test set for one final check. L2 weight decay shrinks weights every step; early stopping returns the parameters with the best validation error; more data shrinks the gap directly.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Processes and limited direct execution
md: A system call is not just a function call. It looks like one because the C library wraps it, but inside is a trap that changes privilege level, and the kernel, not the caller, decides which code runs.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Probability by counting outcomes, and what conditioning does
md: Conditioning means restricting attention to the outcomes consistent with what you know, then renormalizing so they sum to 1. Almost every formula in this course is that one idea applied carefully.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Confidence intervals, p-values and an A/B test
md: Every test in this lesson is the same move: estimate, compute its standard error from the variance rules and the CLT, and ask how many standard errors the estimate sits from the null. Significance depends on sample size as much as on effect size.

courseTitle: Search evaluation basics: precision, recall, MAP, MRR and nDCG
lessonTitle: Why you need a test collection before you can say better
md: Relevance is judged against the **information need**, not the query words. A document that contains every query term can still be nonrelevant, and a document with none of them can be relevant. That is exactly why judgments must come from people and not from term matching.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
md: A bi-encoder trades accuracy for speed in one specific way: the passage vector cannot look at the query. In exchange, every passage is encoded once, ahead of time, and search becomes a nearest-neighbor lookup among vectors. Everything else in this course follows from that trade.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Why language models read subwords, not words or characters
md: A token is not a word. In GPT-2, " hello" (with its leading space) and "hello" are two different tokens with different ids, and many common words are split. Counting words is a poor estimate of token count.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Optimizers: momentum, Adam and decoupled weight decay
md: Adam's step is about **lr in size regardless of gradient scale**. That is its strength, and also why L2 regularization inside Adam misbehaves. Use AdamW when you want weight decay with an adaptive optimizer.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: Building the graph: insertion and the neighbor heuristic
md: Links are bidirectional when added, but pruning (step 4) can later drop a link from one side. The graph is therefore directed in practice, and a node whose incoming links are all pruned becomes hard or impossible to reach. Deletions are hard for the same reason; lesson 5 shows how libraries handle them.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Using synthetic data well: filter, diversify, anchor
md: Synthetic data are useful when an outside signal decides what is kept, diversity is designed in, and real data stay in the training mix. Model collapse is what happens when all three are missing.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: When mmap wins, when it hurts, and how to steer it
md: Use mmap for read-mostly data that fits in memory and benefits from sharing. When data far exceeds memory, or you need control over when writes reach disk and how I/O errors surface, explicit I/O with your own buffer pool wins.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Normalizing partial dates and Present against a reference date
md: A relative expression has no value until it is anchored. *Present*, *now*, *today*, *last year* and *the past 5 years* all need a reference date, and the normalizer should receive it as an explicit input, never read a hidden clock or let a model guess it.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Coverage: how pass@k grows with the number of samples
md: Coverage is an **upper bound** on accuracy. It equals real accuracy only if you have a perfect checker (unit tests, a proof checker). For a math word problem, pass@100 = 83% means 83% of problems have *some* correct sample, not that you can find it.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: A hidden state that is itself a model you train while reading
md: TTT here does not mean fine-tuning the LLM on your prompt. The network's ordinary parameters stay frozen at inference. Only the small per-layer weights $W$ change, they start from $W_0$ for every sequence, and they are discarded afterwards, just like an RNN's hidden state.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: Thrashing at the boundary, and why two magazines bound it at 1/M
md: Two magazines per CPU, one loaded and one previous, guarantee that after every depot trip the CPU holds one full and one empty magazine. That alone bounds depot traffic at 1/M for any workload. Without the previous magazine, an alloc-alloc-free-free loop can send half of all calls to the depot.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
md: Symptoms of thrashing: `pgdemote_*` and `pgpromote_success` both climbing fast at the same time. Pages are moving down and back up. Either the hot set is larger than DRAM, or headroom is too small. Migration itself consumes memory bandwidth on both tiers.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
